To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the resilience of a metapopulations to a drought was enhanced by response diversity among landowners and water sources, (2) a metapopulational rescue effect occurred in the study area, and (3), the CHANS was so complex that metapopulation simulations were unreliable in predicting the impacts of incentive policies on metpopulation persistence.

(1) the black rail is threatened by West Nile virus and the 2012-2015 drought, but the wetland landscape was resilient to the drought due to response diversity in irrigation and landowners’ behaviors, (2) the rescue effect was occurring for both rails, and (3), in dynamic landscapes the rescue effect may not be reliably estimated by occupancy models, metapopulations may be more resilient than expected, and conservation incentive policies may be less effective than expected.

the resilience of the CHANS’ metapopulations to drought is a product of (1) the diversity of landowners’ responses to drought, (2) the heterogeneity of wetlands created by irrigation, and (3a) the rescue effect for black rails and (3b) the resilience of Virginia rails to patch change.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the resilience and dynamics of metapopulatory species in a working landscape and how these dynamics are shaped by the CHANS in which they occur.
how the human transformation of natural systems can create new diversity in the drivers of species dynamics, which can benefit wildlife.

how the interactions among species and humans create complex dynamics and how these dynamics are affected by the behavior and decisions of key actors, and how the resulting feedback loops can create new diversity in the CHANS that may be beneficial for wildlife.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the black rail metacommunity was maintained through the drought of 2012-2015 by the resilience of wetlands, which was in turn maintained by the resilience of the CHANS.
the black rail metacommunity is a metapopulations of wetlands, and wetlands are metapopulations for the black rail, and both are metacommunities in a coupled human and natural system.

The main takeaway from our work is that
conservation of metapopulating species in dynamic landscapes requires a systems approach that accounts for the complex interactions between the species and the CHANS.

conservation in working landscapes requires understanding how the behaviors of humans and wildlife create complex, coupled dynamics that are not predictable from the behavior of the individual species.
CHANS research can be used to identify how the behaviors of actors in working landscapes can be leveraged to improve the persistence of metapopulatons.
